judgment.prompt: The worker saved the same $4,800 and received $500.00 less. Name precisely what caused that, explain why a higher contribution rate produced a worse result, and state which plan rule the worker would have to check to know this could happen.
acceptableAnswerCriteria: Names the cause precisely: the employer contribution is calculated per month with nothing carried forward, so reaching the annual cap in month 8 left 4 months in which no employer contribution could be earned.
Explains the paradox: a higher rate did not increase the amount contributed, because the cap fixes that at $4,800, but it did change the timing, and timing is what the monthly calculation rewards.
Names the rule to check: whether the plan calculates the employer contribution per pay period or across the year — a plan with a year-end true-up would not produce this loss at all.
evidenceRequirements: Uses the $1,000.00 actually earned and the $1,500.00 available, and refers to the 8 contributing months.
lookFors: The response identifies timing rather than amount as the error.
The response notes that the worker did nothing wrong in saving more, only in scheduling it.
judgment.commonMisconception: Assuming that contributing more, or contributing earlier, can only improve the outcome, when a per-period employer calculation rewards contributing in every period instead.

items.promptText: What does the worker contribute each month at 12%?
After how many months is the $4,800 annual cap reached?
What is the largest employer contribution available in a single month?
What employer contribution was earned across the 8 contributing months?
What employer contribution was lost across the remaining months of the year?
What contribution rate would have spread the $4,800 evenly across the whole year, to two decimal places?
What employer contribution would that rate have produced across the year?

The worker saved the same $4,800 and received $500.00 less. Name precisely what caused that, explain why a higher contribution rate produced a worse result, and state which plan rule the worker would have to check to know this could happen.

content.text: t1-p1: What does the worker contribute each month at 12%? Answer: $600.00. Verification: 12% of the $5,000 monthly gross. The rate is applied per month, which is what causes the annual cap to be reached before the year ends. t1-p2: After how many months is the $4,800 annual cap reached? Answer: 8. Verification: $4,800 divided by $600.00 a month. From month 9 onward the worker may contribute nothing further. t1-p3: What is the largest employer contribution available in a single month? Answer: $125.00. Verification: 50% of 5% of $5,000. Because the plan calculates this monthly with nothing carried forward, a month with no worker contribution produces no employer contribution. t2-p1: What employer contribution was earned across the 8 contributing months? Answer: $1,000.00. Verification: $125.00 in each of the 8 months in which the worker contributed at least 5% of pay. t2-p2: What employer contribution was lost across the remaining months of the year? Answer: $500.00. Verification: $125.00 in each of the 4 months with no worker contribution. Nothing was carried forward, so this is not recoverable later in the year. t2-p3: What contribution rate would have spread the $4,800 evenly across the whole year, to two decimal places? Answer: 8.00%. Verification: $4,800 across 12 months is $400.00 a month, which is 8.00% of $5,000. This is above the 5% needed for the full monthly employer contribution, so the cap and the employer terms are compatible at this rate. t2-p4: What employer contribution would that rate have produced across the year? Answer: $1,500.00. Verification: $125.00 in each of 12 months. The worker contributes the same $4,800 either way and receives $500.00 more.
